claims.text: Pearson gave the first formal description in the Philosophical Magazine in 1901, volume 2 of the sixth series, pages 559 to 572, under the title on lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space. His approach was purely geometric: he proposed choosing the line that minimises the squared perpendicular distances from each point to that line.

source.title: Karl Pearson, On lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space, The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, Series 6, 2(11):559-572, 1901, doi 10.1080/14786440109462720

claims.text: Hotelling developed the modern mathematical formulation in the Journal of Educational Psychology in 1933, volume 24, in two parts at pages 417 to 441 and 498 to 520, analysing a complex of statistical variables into principal components.

source.title: Harold Hotelling, Analysis of a complex of statistical variables into principal components, Journal of Educational Psychology 24:417-441 and 498-520, 1933, doi 10.1037/h0071325

beats.broke: many measured variables describe the same few underlying quantities, so the coordinates you were given are more numerous than the structure they carry and are correlated with one another
beats.fix: find the directions along which the points vary most, which are the same directions that minimise the squared perpendicular distances to them, and keep the first few
beats.cost: the directions are chosen by variance, which is a property of the units you happened to measure in, and the resulting axes are combinations of every original variable and so usually mean nothing anybody can name
beats.interview: how this differs from fitting a line by regression
